title: Another person dies after jail time
article: For the second time this month, a person has died after being in police custody.

Albert William Prevost was taken from cells by ambulance March 14th after spending the night in jail for public intoxication, says a press release from Island District RCMP. Upon speaking with Mr. Prevost, an RCMP member became concerned "that a medical issue may be present."
Mr. Prevost was transported by ambulance to Port Hardy hospital and then was subsequently transferred to Campbell River hospital where he died nine days later on March 23.
The cause of his death is under investigation by the BC Coroner's Service.

This is the second death this month for a prisoner. Debbie Coon died early in March after being jailed for causing a disturbance at the hospital and apparent intoxication. After hitting her head in the cell, she was returned to the hospital by ambulance, then transferred to Victoria where she later died.
Last September, another man picked up for public intoxication died after hitting his head while in the cells in Port Hardy.

"That is part of the reason the Integrated Major Crime Unit is involved in the investigation," says Cst. Darren Lagan, RCMP media spokesperson for Island District. "They are looking into each of the incidents. But I can tell you there is no evident relationship between the three deaths."
Lagan adds there is video surveillance of the cells for each incident that has been turned over to the B.C. Coroner Service for their investigation.
Staff Sargeant Chris Stewart of the Port Hardy detachment is taking steps to deal with the problem.

"As a result of the tragic deaths, I have arranged a meeting with VIHA, Mental Health and other interested agencies to discuss alternative ways of dealing with people with addicition issues," said Stewart. "We are really looking for ways to avoid future incidents."
Lagan says RCMP officers take a risk when they incarcerate intoxicated individuals.

"These people could have medical conditions we don't know about. What did they take? What did they ingest before they came in? We don't know but we take that risk whenever someone is put in cells," said Lagan.
Lagan says Port Hardy detachment has a reputation of treating prisoners well.

"They probably have one of the best cellblocks on the Island," said Lagan. "In most places ... they get put in a cement room to sleep it off. In Port Hardy, they get blankets, socks if they need them, a meal if they haven't eaten and a cup of coffee before they leave in the morning. They really go above and beyond what's dictated."
